MRCS Part A · Section A Basic Science · Anatomy · Chapter 1

Upper Limb Anatomy

Revision pack for Chapter 1 of MRCS IV Courses, Part A (6th ed., 2025), book pages 1–38. Summary with the book's own figures, mind maps, 40 chapter MCQs, and an Egyptian Fellowship (الزمالة المصرية) section with exam facts and 15 practice questions.

Chapter 1
1

Landmarks of the upper limb

Book pp. 2–5

Clavicle and scalene muscles

  • In front of scalenus anterior (just behind the clavicle): subclavian vein and phrenic nerve.
  • Between scalenus anterior and medius: subclavian artery and the roots of the brachial plexus.
  • The sternoclavicular joint lies in front of the origin of the subclavian artery.

Deltopectoral groove and coracoid process

  • The groove between deltoid and pectoralis major carries the cephalic vein.
  • An incision from below the sternoclavicular joint to the deltopectoral groove can injure the thoracoacromial artery. The shoulder capsule, plexus roots and trunks, and pectoralis minor insertion are safe.
  • Surface marking of the coracoid: 1 cm below the junction of the medial ¾ and lateral ¼ of the clavicle.
  • Attached to the coracoid: ligaments coracoclavicular, coracohumeral, coracoacromial; muscles pectoralis minor (insertion), coracobrachialis and short head of biceps (origins).

Humerus

LandmarkRelated structure
Anatomical neckAttachment of the shoulder joint capsule
Surgical neckAxillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery
Greater and lesser tuberositiesRotator cuff insertions
Bicipital grooveTLP, medial → lateral: teres major (medial lip), latissimus dorsi (floor), pectoralis major (lateral lip)
Spiral grooveRadial nerve + profunda brachii artery
Medial epicondyleCommon flexor origin: pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FDS, FCU

Radius, elbow and radioulnar joints

  • Lister's tubercle on the distal radius: the EPL tendon hooks around it and can be trapped there.
  • Elbow has 3 articulations: radial head with capitulum; trochlea with trochlear notch of ulna; olecranon with olecranon fossa.
  • Superior radioulnar joint: radial head with radial notch of ulna, held by the annular ligament. Inferior: ulnar head with ulnar notch of radius. Together they allow pronation and supination.

Carpal bones

  • Proximal row (lateral → medial): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.
  • Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
  • Scaphoid: most commonly fractured. Its blood (radial artery) enters the distal end, so the proximal pole is prone to avascular necrosis. Articulates with 5 bones: radius, lunate, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate.
  • Lunate: most commonly dislocated; compresses the median nerve.
  • Pisiform: sesamoid bone inside the FCU tendon.
  • 14 phalanges per hand (thumb has 2).
Check

The book calls the scaphoid the largest carpal bone. The capitate is the largest overall; the scaphoid is the largest of the proximal row.

High-yield

Saddle: sternoclavicular and thumb CMC. Pivot: both radioulnar joints. Ellipsoid: wrist and MCP. The shoulder is one of the least stable joints (lax capsule, shallow glenoid); the rotator cuff is its main stabiliser (p. 18).

3

Brachial plexus

Book pp. 7–8

Formation

  • Roots: C5, C6, C7, C8, T1.
  • Trunks: upper (C5 + C6), middle (C7 alone), lower (C8 + T1).
  • Divisions: each trunk splits into anterior and posterior.
  • Cords: posterior = all 3 posterior divisions; lateral = anterior divisions of upper + middle trunks (C5–7); medial = anterior division of lower trunk (C8–T1).

Relations

  • Roots: behind scalenus anterior, in the posterior triangle.
  • Trunks: related to the subclavian artery.
  • Divisions: behind the middle third of the clavicle.
  • Cords: around the axillary artery in the axilla.

Branches

FromBranches
RootsDorsal scapular n. to Rhomboids (C5) · long thoracic n. to Serratus anterior (C5, 6, 7) · nerves to Scalenes (all roots)
Upper trunkSuprascapular n. · nerve to Subclavius ("2S")
Lateral cord (C5–7)Lateral pectoral n. · musculocutaneous n. · lateral root of median n.
Medial cord (C8–T1)Medial pectoral n. · medial cutaneous n. of arm · medial cutaneous n. of forearm · medial root of median n. · ulnar n.
Posterior cord ("ULNAR")Upper subscapular · Lower subscapular · Nerve to latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal) · Axillary · Radial (continuation of the cord)
Check

The book also lists a "lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm" under the lateral cord. The lateral cutaneous nerves of the arm come from the axillary (upper) and radial (lower) nerves; the lateral cord's branches are the three above.

Clinical

Pancoast tumour (lung apex, superior sulcus syndrome) grows up into the lower trunk: small-muscle wasting of the hand ± Horner's syndrome. A posterior cord injury gives combined radial + axillary deficits.

Concept: joint balance

Flexors and extensors are matched in power. When one group is weakened, the joint is pulled towards the intact side. This explains the resting deformities in plexus and nerve injuries.

Forearm: rules that answer most questions

  • Any superficialis or brevis inserts into the middle phalanx; any profundus or longus into the distal phalanx. Exceptions: APL → 1st metacarpal; APB → proximal phalanx of thumb.
  • Any ulnaris muscle also deviates the wrist ulnarly (adduction); any radialis muscle deviates radially (abduction).

Exam trap

Adductor pollicis sits among the thenar muscles but is not one of them, and it is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Book pp. 24–25

Cutaneous nerves

  • Skin over deltoid (badge area): axillary n., C5.
  • Armpit: intercostobrachial n.
  • Medial arm and forearm: medial cutaneous nn. of arm and forearm.
  • Posterior arm and forearm: posterior cutaneous nn. (radial).
  • Lateral arm: upper and lower lateral cutaneous nn. of arm.
  • Lateral forearm: musculocutaneous n. (lateral cutaneous n. of forearm).

  • Ulnar: medial ⅓ of hand + medial 1½ fingers (palm and dorsum).
  • Median: lateral ⅔ of palm + lateral 3½ fingers (palmar side), plus the distal phalanges of those fingers on the dorsum.
  • Radial: lateral ⅔ of dorsum + lateral 3½ fingers (dorsal side), except the distal phalanges.

7

Nerve injuries of the upper limb

Book pp. 26–29, 38

Upper trunk (C5–6): Erb–Duchenne palsy

Also called the policeman's / porter's / waiter's tip position.

DeformityMuscles paralysedNerve
Arm adductedSupraspinatus, deltoidSuprascapular, axillary
Arm internally rotatedInfraspinatus, teres minorSuprascapular, axillary
Forearm extendedBiceps, brachialisMusculocutaneous
Forearm pronatedBrachioradialis (and biceps as supinator)Radial (musculocutaneous)
Wrist flexedExtensor carpi radialis longusRadial
Sensory lossLateral arm (lateral cutaneous n. of arm) and lateral forearm (musculocutaneous)

Only the medial cord (lower trunk) branches work fully.

Lower trunk (C8–T1): Klumpke's paralysis ± Horner's syndrome

DeformityMuscles paralysedNerve
Wasting of hand muscles, loss of fine movementsMedial half of FDP, interossei and lumbricalsUlnar + partly median
Wrist extended
Claw: MCP hyperextended, IP flexed
Sensory lossMedial arm, forearm (medial cutaneous nn.) and hand (ulnar)

Only the lateral cord (upper trunk) branches work fully. Horner's (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) appears when T1 sympathetic fibres are involved.

Ulnar nerve: the ulnar paradox

Clawing shows when the patient tries to extend the fingers. The lower the lesion, the worse the claw, because FDP (medial half) still works and pulls the fingers into flexion.

LevelFlexorsIntrinsicsSensoryResult
ElbowMedial FDP + FCU paralysedMedial 2 lumbricals paralysedPalmar and dorsal medial hand lostPartial claw
Forearm (book)Medial FDP + FCU paralysedMedial 2 lumbricals paralysedPalmar lost, dorsal intactPartial claw
WristFDP + FCU intactMedial 2 lumbricals paralysedPalmar medial 1½ lost, dorsal intactComplete claw
Froment's test

Patient grips paper between thumb and index finger. With adductor pollicis paralysed (ulnar), the thumb IP joint flexes (FPL, median) to hold it: positive.

Sign of benediction (median / AIN)

On making a fist, ring and little fingers flex (ulnar half of FDP) but index and middle stay straight (median/AIN half).

8

Vessels of the upper limb

Book pp. 30–31

Axillary artery

  • Starts at the outer border of the 1st rib (continuation of the subclavian). Ends at the lower border of teres major (becomes brachial).
  • 1st part (medial to pec minor): superior thoracic.
  • 2nd part (behind): thoracoacromial (acromiothoracic) + lateral thoracic.
  • 3rd part (lateral): subscapular (gives circumflex scapular) + anterior and posterior circumflex humeral.

Brachial artery

  • Starts at the lower border of teres major; ends in the cubital fossa as radial and ulnar arteries (ulnar is larger).
  • Branches: profunda brachii (largest), superior and inferior ulnar collaterals.
  • At the wrist the ulnar artery lies nearer the midline and the ulnar nerve outside it: the nerve is medial to the artery.

Superficial veins

Cephalic veinBasilic vein
StartLateral end of dorsal venous archMedial end of dorsal venous arch
ForearmLateral sideMedial side
Cubital fossaJoined by the subcutaneous median cubital vein
EndDeltopectoral groove → pierces clavipectoral fascia → axillary veinPierces deep fascia → becomes the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major
9

Important regions

Book pp. 32–37

Breast

  • Lies on pectoralis major and serratus anterior.
  • Arterial supply: mainly internal mammary a.; intercostal aa.; thoracoacromial a. (short trunk from the front of the 2nd part of the axillary a., at risk when exposing the axillary artery).
  • At risk in mastectomy: intercostobrachial n. (armpit sensation; may be sacrificed), long thoracic n. (winged scapula), thoracodorsal bundle (latissimus dorsi).

Axilla

  • Apex: 1st rib, scapula, clavicle · Base: axillary fascia.
  • Anterior: pec major, pec minor, subclavius · Posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi.
  • Lateral: humerus · Medial: serratus anterior + chest wall.
  • Contents: axillary artery and vein, plexus cords, lymph nodes.
  • Nodes: anterior (pectoral, first from breast), posterior (subscapular, scapular region), lateral (humeral, arm), central (from the first three), apical (from all).
  • Levels by pec minor (see the node-level figure in section 8): I below/lateral, II behind, III above/medial.

Posterior scapular spaces

SpaceBoundariesContents
QuadrangularSup: teres minor · Inf: teres major · Lat: humerus · Med: long head of tricepsAxillary n. + posterior circumflex humeral a. (same pair wind round the surgical neck)
Upper (medial) triangularSup: teres minor · Inf: teres major · Lat: long head of tricepsCircumflex scapular a.
Lower (lateral) triangularSup: teres major · Lat: humerus · Med: long head of tricepsRadial n. + profunda brachii a. (same pair run in the spiral groove)

Cubital fossa

  • Lateral: brachioradialis · Medial: pronator teres · Superior: line between the humeral epicondyles.
  • Contents, medial → lateral: median n., brachial a., biceps tendon, radial n.
  • Roof: lateral cutaneous n. of forearm (end of musculocutaneous n.).

Anatomical snuff box

  • Posteromedial: EPL · Anterolateral: EPB + APL.
  • Floor: scaphoid and trapezium (tenderness = suspect scaphoid fracture).
  • Contents: radial artery, cephalic vein, superficial radial nerve.

Flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel)

  • Attachments: lateral to scaphoid + trapezium; medial to pisiform + hamate.
  • Deep to it: median n. (commonest entrapment site), FDS, FDP, FPL, FCR.
  • Superficial to it: ulnar n., ulnar vessels, palmar branch of ulnar n., palmar branch of median n., palmaris longus.
Exam trap

In carpal tunnel syndrome, sensation over the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the retinaculum.

Extensor retinaculum

Hand grip (prehension)

Precision grip · ulnar + median

Small, often fragile objects; uses the small hand muscles.
1. Terminal opposition (pincer, holding a pin): finest.
2. Subterminal opposition: commonest.
3. Subtermino-lateral (key grip): less fine, strong.
4. Adduction grip (index–middle, no thumb): weak.

Power grip · ulnar + median + radial

1. Palmar grip: most powerful.
2. Hook grip: object held between palm and flexed fingers, thumb not used (carrying bags).

The radial nerve matters because wrist extension makes the finger flexors stronger.

Egyptian Fellowship / Egyptian Board · الزمالة المصرية / البورد المصري

Egyptian Fellowship: the exam

Researched on 17 Nov 2026 from the Egyptian Health Council (EHC) and secondary sites. Each card says how well the fact is supported. Confirm dates and fees in your EHC trainee account or with your training centre.

Confirmed · EHC

Who runs it

The Egyptian Health Council (المجلس الصحي المصري), under Law 12/2022 and Prime Ministerial Decree 3798/2023. The certificate is now called the Egyptian Board (البورد المصري); the Fellowship programme continued under the EHC in 2022. Candidates still use both names.

Confirmed · EHC framework

Three parts

Part 1: written MCQ on the basic sciences and skills of the specialty, possibly computer-based; a council may add an oral or practical. Part 2: written MCQ on clinical topics plus applied basic science. Part 3: OSCE / OSPE / data stations, possibly with orals and cases, over 2–4 days.

Confirmed · dates vary

When it runs

The framework sets Part 1 in March and August, Part 2 in April and September, Part 3 once a year (Dec/Jan). Recent rounds have moved: the EHC Board site posted results for a Part 1 "August 2026 round" during Sep–Nov 2026.

Confirmed · EHC framework

Eligibility for Part 1

At least 3 months into Egyptian Board training, TOEFL score of 500 or more, ICDL certificate, and exam fees paid.

Confirmed · EHC framework

Attempts and pass mark

Up to 6 attempts at Part 1; not passing within that limit means leaving the programme. There is no fixed pass percentage: written papers are standard-set by Angoff, modified Angoff or Hofstee.

Not published

Paper format for General Surgery

Each specialty council sets the number of questions, duration and blueprint. None is published for General Surgery, and the option count (4 or 5) is not confirmed. This pack uses 5-option single-best-answer questions, as in MRCS Part A.

Partly confirmed

MRCS and exemptions

Part 1 exemption is confirmed for a Master's, MD or Arab Board in the same specialty, and for a full UK Royal College fellowship in the same specialty (applied for within 5 years). We found no official rule that MRCS exempts you from Part 1.

Confirmed · EHC framework

Confidentiality

Publishing exam content, including posting details online, counts as misconduct with possible 1–2 year bans. This is why reliable recall papers are not available online.

No verified recall list

Past-paper themes

We searched English and Arabic sources (recalls, Telegram and Facebook summaries, prep sites) and found no verified list of upper-limb topics from previous Egyptian Fellowship / Board papers. The list below is the high-yield core of this chapter that MCQ basic-science papers (MRCS Part A and board Part 1 exams) test again and again. Use it as a priority list, not as a recall.

15 clinical-scenario SBAs · written for this pack

Fellowship-style practice

Applied-anatomy questions in the style of a board Part 1 paper. They are not recalled exam questions.
